title: CQC, clinical governance & regulation
blurb: Who regulates what in UK dentistry, CQC's five key questions, the devolved regulators, and how clinical governance and audit keep standards rising.
question: A CQC inspector visits your practice in England and asks how the practice knows its staff are trained and competent, and how it learns from audits and incidents. Which of CQC's key questions are they exploring, and how is CQC's role different from the GDC's?

teach.h: People and places are regulated separately
teach.body: The General Dental Council (GDC) regulates dental PROFESSIONALS across the whole UK: it registers dentists and dental care professionals, sets the Standards for the Dental Team and CPD requirements, and deals with fitness to practise. The practice itself, as a healthcare PROVIDER, is regulated by a different body. In England that is the Care Quality Commission (CQC). Dental practices in England must register with CQC under the Health and Social Care Act 2008 and meet its fundamental standards.

head: Body
Regulates
Dental example
teach.caption: NHS dental services are commissioned (paid for and planned) separately from regulation. In England, local integrated care boards commission NHS dentistry.

letters.sub: Infection control, medical emergencies, safeguarding, radiation safety
Evidence-based care, trained and competent staff, valid consent
Access, meeting individual needs, handling complaints

teach.caption: Inspectors use these five questions to judge any service CQC regulates. Training records feed into 'effective'; audits and learning from incidents feed into 'well-led'.

teach.body: CQC's fundamental standards are the standards below which care must never fall. They include person-centred care, dignity and respect, consent, safe care and treatment, safeguarding from abuse, safe premises and equipment, handling complaints, good governance, enough suitably qualified staff, fit and proper persons employed, and the duty of candour: being open and honest with patients when something goes wrong. CQC can take enforcement action, including prosecution, when standards aren't met.

teach.caption: HIW = Healthcare Inspectorate Wales. HIS = Healthcare Improvement Scotland, which regulates independent (private) clinics; NHS practices in Scotland are also inspected by their NHS health board. RQIA = Regulation and Quality Improvement Authority.

teach.body: Clinical governance is the framework through which a practice is accountable for continuously improving the quality of its care and safeguarding high standards. It is usually taught as a set of pillars: clinical audit, risk management, clinical effectiveness (evidence-based practice), education and training, patient and public involvement (feedback and complaints), staffing and staff management, and information management (records). As a dental nurse you take part by following policies, joining audits, reporting incidents, keeping records well and keeping your training up to date.

teach.caption: Examples: infection control audit every 6 months (HTM 01-05); radiograph quality audit against the targets of at least 95% grade A for digital and 90% for film.

teach.h: Evidence an inspector will look for
teach.body: Inspectors want evidence, not promises. A practice keeps a record of who has completed which training (medical emergencies, infection control, safeguarding, radiography, fire) to show staff are competent for their tasks. Staff files typically hold GDC registration checks, indemnity, hepatitis B immunity and DBS checks. Policies, risk assessments, audits with action plans, maintenance logs, and records of incidents and complaints with the learning from them all show the practice is safe and well-led.

teach.text: GDC regulates PEOPLE (UK-wide). CQC regulates the PRACTICE (England only). If a question is about an individual nurse's fitness to practise, it's the GDC; if it's about the practice's registration or inspection in England, it's CQC.

items: GDC: dental professionals, UK-wide. CQC: providers in England.
CQC five key questions: Safe, Effective, Caring, Responsive, Well-led.
Fundamental standards include safe care, safeguarding, consent, governance, staffing and the duty of candour.
Devolved regulators: HIW (Wales), HIS (Scotland), RQIA (Northern Ireland).
Clinical governance: audit, risk management, evidence-based care, training, patient involvement, staffing, records.
Training records prove competence; audits and learning from incidents prove the practice is well-led.

summary: You can now explain the difference between the GDC and CQC, name CQC's five key questions and the devolved regulators, describe clinical governance and the audit cycle, and show what evidence a practice keeps to prove it is safe and well-led.

A.q: An inspector asks how the practice knows its staff can carry out their duties safely. Why should the practice keep records of who has had which training?
options: To work out staff holiday entitlement
To decide which members of staff are paid the most
To show staff are competent for their tasks
A.why: Training records are evidence that staff are trained and competent for what they do, which inspectors check.

whyNot.0: Holiday entitlement isn't linked to training records.
whyNot.1: Pay decisions are not the purpose of training records.
whyNot.3: Accountants aren't concerned with clinical competence.

A.q: Which body regulates dental practices as healthcare providers in England?
A.why: CQC registers and inspects health and social care providers in England, including dental practices.

whyNot.0: The GDC regulates individual dental professionals, not the practice.
whyNot.1: HIW regulates healthcare services in Wales.
whyNot.2: The BDA is a professional association and trade union.

A.q: Which of these is NOT one of CQC's five key questions?
A.why: The five key questions are safe, effective, caring, responsive and well-led. Profit is not one of them.

whyNot.0: Safe is one of the five key questions.
whyNot.1: Well-led is one of the five key questions.
whyNot.3: Responsive is one of the five key questions.

B.q: A dental practice in Cardiff is inspected by which regulator?
B.why: Healthcare Inspectorate Wales (HIW) regulates and inspects healthcare services in Wales.

B.q: The practice carries out an infection control audit and finds gaps. According to the audit cycle, what comes next?
options: File the results and wait a year
Send the results to the GDC
B.why: After comparing practice with the standard, the team makes changes and then re-audits to check they worked.

whyNot.0: Doing nothing defeats the purpose of audit.
whyNot.2: Lowering the standard to match poor practice isn't improvement.
whyNot.3: Audit results are used within the practice, not routinely sent to the GDC.

B.q: Which body would deal with concerns about an individual dental nurse's fitness to practise?
B.why: The GDC registers dental professionals and investigates their fitness to practise.

whyNot.0: CQC regulates the practice as a provider, not individual registrants.
whyNot.1: HSE enforces workplace health and safety law.
whyNot.2: The MHRA regulates medicines and medical devices.

C.q: Under which of CQC's key questions would inspectors mainly look at leadership, governance and audit?
C.why: Well-led covers leadership, governance, audit and the culture of the practice.

whyNot.0: Caring is about kindness, dignity and involving patients.
whyNot.1: Responsive is about access, individual needs and complaints.
whyNot.2: Effective is about evidence-based care, outcomes and competent staff.

options: A framework for improving quality and safety
The practice's financial accounts and payroll system
C.why: Clinical governance is the framework through which a practice continuously improves quality and keeps standards high.

whyNot.1: Financial accounts are separate from clinical governance.
whyNot.2: Fee scales are about payment, not quality improvement.
whyNot.3: GDC fitness to practise is professional regulation, not governance within the practice.

C.q: Which regulator inspects private dental practices in Northern Ireland?
C.why: The Regulation and Quality Improvement Authority (RQIA) is the independent health and social care regulator in Northern Ireland.

whyNot.3: The GDC regulates individual professionals, not practices.

reteach.title: The driver and the garage
reteach.question: Think of a garage that services cars. Mechanics need their own qualifications, and the garage itself needs to be safe and well run. Who checks which?

blocks.body: The GDC is like the body that licenses each mechanic: it checks you are qualified, keeps you on the register, and can remove you if you're unsafe, wherever you work in the UK. CQC is like the inspector who checks the garage: is it safe, are the staff trained, is it well managed, does it treat customers well, does it fix complaints? In Wales, Scotland and Northern Ireland, a different garage inspector does that job.

blocks.text: Remember the five key questions as S-E-C-R-W: Safe, Effective, Caring, Responsive, Well-led.

explain.body: GDC: dental professionals, UK-wide. CQC: providers in England. HSE: workplace safety. MHRA: medicines and devices. ICO: data protection.

test.q: A practice in Manchester wants to start providing dental care. Which body must it register with as a provider?
test.why: Dental practices in England must register with CQC as healthcare providers.

whyNot.0: The GDC registers individual professionals, not practices.
whyNot.1: ICO registration may be needed for data, but it doesn't replace CQC registration.
whyNot.2: HSE enforces health and safety law but doesn't register providers.

explain.body: Safe, Effective, Caring, Responsive, Well-led. Every piece of evidence an inspector looks at feeds into one or more of these.

test.q: An inspector reviews how the practice handles and learns from complaints, and whether patients can get urgent appointments. Which key question is this?
test.why: Responsive covers access to care, meeting individual needs and handling complaints.

whyNot.1: Safe covers infection control, emergencies and safeguarding.
whyNot.2: Caring covers kindness, dignity and involvement.
whyNot.3: Effective covers evidence-based care and staff competence.

explain.body: England: CQC. Wales: Healthcare Inspectorate Wales. Scotland: Healthcare Improvement Scotland (independent clinics), with NHS health boards inspecting NHS practices. Northern Ireland: RQIA. The GDC covers everyone.

test.q: What does the abbreviation HIW stand for?
test.why: HIW is Healthcare Inspectorate Wales, the independent inspector of healthcare in Wales.

whyNot.0: Close, but the name is Healthcare Inspectorate Wales.
whyNot.2: This is not a real body.
whyNot.3: HIW covers all healthcare services, not just hospitals.

explain.body: Clinical governance is how the practice keeps improving quality and safety: audit, risk management, evidence-based care, training, patient involvement, staffing and records. Audit runs in a cycle: set a standard, measure, compare, change, re-audit.

test.q: How often does HTM 01-05 expect a practice to audit its infection control and decontamination?
test.why: HTM 01-05 expects an infection control audit every six months.

whyNot.0: Monthly isn't the HTM 01-05 audit interval.
whyNot.1: Three years is far too long.
whyNot.3: Audit is routine and preventive, not only reactive.
